name: Tomas Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's my family's farm, Greystone, a hundred and twenty hectares with a few beef cattle, a flock of laying hens, some potatoes and cereals, and the thing that pays the bills, the farm shop on Station Road. I'm up at six for the animals, then by nine I'm in the shop checking the night's online orders on my phone. Four people work in the shop and two on the land, and I'm the one who answers to all of them. My mum still does the books on Tuesdays, which is an argument every week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because I've moved everything onto a tablet and she still wants the paper ledger. I use an AI tool every day: it writes the shop's posts, it helps me plan the stock for the weekend, it turns my voice notes into the staff rota. Mum says I talk to my phone more than to her, and she's not entirely wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love Saturday mornings in the shop, when people come in and tell me the sausages were the best they've had. It's the only bit of farming where somebody says thank you to your face. What wears me out is that we borrowed for the shop and the cold room, so every penny goes back in. We've got less than a month of savings, and Hanna's nursing shifts are what stop us going under some months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's brilliant and anyone not using it is missing out. I'd probably show people at the farmers' market how I do the rota in two minutes. Some of them would roll their eyes, but that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really think it's good news for me, a small helper that's getting better. The risk for my business isn't AI, it's the supermarket opening a big store on the ring road. If everything else carries on as normal, I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push it further, maybe get it to handle customer emails and suggest what to price the lamb at. I'd budget maybe thirty a month for a better version. I'd also show Priya in the shop how to use it, because she's quick and she'd take some load off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It feels like having one more pair of hands for the price of a takeaway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend thirty a month. With savings as thin as they are, is that a stretch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a stretch, but it pays back. If it saves me three hours a week, that's three hours I'm with the kids or in the shop selling. I'd rather cut my coffee habit than cut that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks it'll make us lazy. Her dad farmed with one tractor and a notebook in his shirt pocket. I tell her he'd have loved this, he was always the first to buy anything new at the show. She just says, he also nearly went bankrupt twice.

S0.say: I'd say it's brilliant and anyone not using it is missing out. I'd show people at the farmers' market how I do the rota in two minutes, even if some rolled their eyes.
S0.think: I think it's good news, a small helper getting better. The real risk to my business isn't AI, it's a big supermarket opening on the ring road.
S0.do: Extends AI to customer emails and lamb pricing, budgeting about thirty a month for a better version. Trains Priya in the shop to use it so she can take on some of his load.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like having an extra pair of hands cheaply.
S0.quote: She just says, he also nearly went bankrupt twice.
S0.fieldNote: He's an early adopter in his bones and talks about AI like a new tractor. His mother acts as the family's brake, and he enjoys the argument. The thin savings don't slow him down; he treats spending on tools as an investment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for small farms to punch above their weight, if the tools stay cheap and the government helps people get started. But I'd also say firms hiring fewer beginners is a scandal. Somebody has to train the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this suits me fine. Slow change is the kind I can ride. The thing that worries me is my two shop staff in their twenties, Priya and Josh, and what happens to young people round here if the town firms stop taking them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up to the government's small-business AI scheme if there was one, and I'd take on an apprentice in the shop, even if it cost me. Maybe I'd offer Josh a proper apprenticeship in butchery with the local college, about two days a month away. I'd write about it online so other farm shops did the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little knot about the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprentice costs money you don't really have. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's usually a grant for half, and the rest I'd find by not replacing the old chiller for another year. That chiller makes a noise like a dying cow, but it works. I'd rather have Josh learning than a quiet fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did someone give you a start like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Ken, the butcher in town, let me hang around his shop when I was fifteen. He taught me to bone out a lamb shoulder with my eyes half shut. He's dead now, and that shop's a phone repair place.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for small farms to punch above their weight if tools stay cheap and the government helps. But firms hiring fewer beginners is a scandal, because someone has to train the next lot.
S1.think: I think slow change suits me fine, since it's the kind I can ride. My worry is for my young shop staff and for local young people if town firms stop taking them on.
S1.do: Joins any small-business AI scheme on offer and offers his shop worker Josh a butchery apprenticeship with the local college, funding half by grant and half by delaying a new chiller for a year.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small knot of worry about young people.
S1.quote: That chiller makes a noise like a dying cow, but it works. I'd rather have Josh learning than a quiet fridge.
S1.fieldNote: He turns the scenario into something to act on immediately, and his progressive views show as hands-on mentoring rather than slogans. The story of Ken the butcher explains why he cares about first jobs. He takes a small financial risk without hesitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people losing office jobs need real help, not a lecture about learning new skills. I'd back a tax on the AI firms to pay for retraining. And I'd say shop local, because every pound that stays in town matters more when money's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my customers are exactly those office people. The solicitor's wife who buys the expensive beef every Friday, the insurance man who orders a box every month. If they're worried about their jobs, they shop at the discount store, and my takings drop. That's my real risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a cheaper range in the shop within three months, mince, sausages, a value veg box, so people who are worried about money still come in. I'd use the AI to track which customers stop coming and send them a friendly note. And I'd look at selling to the school kitchens, which is steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm still in control, but I'd be watching the till like a hawk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd send a note to customers who stop coming. Some people might find that a bit much. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, Hanna said the same. I'd keep it simple, a voucher and a hello, written by me, checked by the machine. Nothing that sounds like a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling to the school kitchens, how would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council buys for six schools in our area. Leo's school serves frozen burgers from a factory three countries away. If I could get a contract for even one meal a week, it'd cover a shop worker's wages, and my son would eat our own beef at lunch.

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs need real help, not lectures on new skills, and I'd back a tax on AI firms to pay for retraining. I'd also urge people to shop local while money's tight.
S2.think: I think my customers are exactly those office workers, like the solicitor's wife and the insurance man. If they fear for their jobs they'll shop at the discount store and my takings will drop.
S2.do: Adds a cheaper range within three months, uses AI to spot lapsed customers and send them a simple voucher, and bids to supply local school kitchens for at least one meal a week.
S2.feel: Uneasy but in control, watching the till closely.
S2.quote: Leo's school serves frozen burgers from a factory three countries away.
S2.fieldNote: He's the first of these farmers to see his own customers as the people losing office jobs. He moves fast with practical fixes and takes my pushback about the customer notes well. The school kitchen idea mixes business, local pride and his son's lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're watching the biggest transfer of wealth in my lifetime, and it's going the wrong way. People who own shares and houses get richer while the ones who did the work lose it. I'd say it plainly in the shop, and if some customers didn't like it, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened for the shop more than the farm. If lots of professionals lose their jobs, the Saturday crowd shrinks by half. We borrowed against the land for the shop, so if takings fall for a year, we're in real trouble, and my mum would never say I told you so, but she'd think it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bank in the first month, before they come to me, and ask to stretch the loan. I'd cut the shop to five days and do the sixth day on the stall at the city market, where the people with share money are. I'd use the AI to model the worst case, every number, so I'm not guessing at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, planning, but there's a cold feeling under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said share and house prices boom. Does any of that reach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a bit. We own the land, but you can't eat land, and selling it would end the farm. The only boom we'd feel is the price of a house for Elsa one day, which would go out of reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell at the city market to the people doing well. How does that sit with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkwardly. I'd be selling posh sausages to the winners while I'm saying they should pay more tax. But I'd say it to them too, I'm not shy. And the money keeps my staff paid.

S3.say: I'd say we're watching the biggest transfer of wealth in my lifetime, going the wrong way to people who own shares and houses. I'd say it plainly in the shop and not mind who disliked it.
S3.think: I think I'm frightened for the shop more than the farm, as the Saturday crowd could halve. We borrowed against the land for it, so a year of lower takings would put us in real trouble.
S3.do: Goes to the bank in the first month to stretch the loan, cuts the shop to five days and takes a stall at the city market, and uses AI to model the worst case in detail.
S3.feel: Anxious and busy planning, with a cold feeling underneath.
S3.quote: I'd be selling posh sausages to the winners while I'm saying they should pay more tax.
S3.fieldNote: The loan against the land makes him far more exposed than his cheerfulness suggests. He moves before the bank does, which fits his risk-tolerant style. He named the contradiction in selling to the winners himself before I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms could be fine if farmers and workers own them together, like the old machinery co-ops. If big firms own them and rent them out, we're just tenants on our own land. I'd push for co-ops loudly, in the farmers' union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm half ready and half scared. I'd love a robot that feeds the hens and weeds the potatoes. But if robots are in shops and kitchens too, the supermarket gets cheaper and cheaper, and a farm shop's whole point is people. And if everyone round here is out of work, nobody's buying my beef.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to be one of the first farms in the county with a shared robot, through a co-op with three or four neighbours, to keep costs down. I'd move my two farm staff onto the shop and deliveries, because people still want a person. I'd also ask Hanna whether she could take on more nursing shifts, as care homes would need people managing the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a sort of reckless energy. Like the first day of harvest when the weather's turning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be one of the first with a robot, with less than a month saved. What if it goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have made a big mistake, and it wouldn't be my first. That's why I'd do it with neighbours, so the risk is split four ways. My granddad bought the first combine in the valley with two other farmers, and they shared it for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elsa and Leo about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the farm will look different but it's still ours, and they'd need to learn both, the cows and the code. Elsa already asks the AI how cows digest grass. I'd want them to know their way round a shed before a screen.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots could be fine if farmers and workers own them together, like the old machinery co-ops. If big firms own and rent them, we're tenants on our own land, and I'd push that hard.
S4.think: I think I'm half ready and half scared. I'd welcome a robot to feed hens and weed potatoes, but cheaper supermarkets and local job losses could empty the farm shop.
S4.do: Forms a co-op with three or four neighbours to share one of the county's first farm robots, moves his farm staff onto the shop and deliveries, and asks his partner about extra nursing shifts.
S4.feel: Anxious, but with a reckless energy, like the first day of harvest with the weather turning.
S4.quote: If big firms own them and rent them out, we're just tenants on our own land.
S4.fieldNote: Even in the hardest scenario he's looking for the move, not the exit. His family history of shared machinery shapes his co-op answer. Under the energy there's a real fear that the shop, which is about people, loses its point.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the third, oddly, more than the robots. Robots I can try to get ahead of. But if my customers lose their jobs and the bank calls in the loan, there's nothing clever I can do about it. What would help is the bank being made to give small businesses a year's breathing room, and the government putting money in people's pockets so they can still buy local.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the mums. My mum, I mean, and the older farmers. Everyone talks about young people and AI, but my mum's seventy-one and she's frightened of all of it. She'd be the one who'd feel the farm was lost even if we saved it.

headlineQuote: If big firms own them and rent them out, we're just tenants on our own land.
portrait: Tomas Larsen, 43, runs his family's mixed farm and the farm shop on Station Road that pays the bills, with six staff and a loan against the land. He uses AI every day and treats each new tool as an extra pair of hands, while his mother keeps the paper ledger and warns him. Across the scenarios he moves fast: apprenticeships, a cheaper shop range, bank talks and a city market stall, a robot shared through a neighbours' co-op. What frightens him is not the technology but his customers losing their jobs while he has borrowed heavily and saved little.
biggestWorry: The fast AI picture worries him most, more than the robots, because he can't outmanoeuvre his customers losing their jobs while the bank holds a loan against the land.
whatWouldHelp: Rules giving small businesses a year's breathing room on loans, and money in people's pockets so they can still buy local.
